notes.meaning: Amos announces a warning of sorrow on the leaders of both Judah in Zion and Israel in Samaria. These wealthy rulers felt safe behind their fortified city walls and high social status, so they ignored the Lord's warnings. Their pride and false sense of security blinded them to the danger hanging over their nations.

differ.view: Some Baptists apply this warning to churchgoers who feel a false spiritual security, resting on outward church membership instead of true repentance.

notes.meaning: God tells the leaders to look at three great neighboring cities: Calneh, Hamath, and Gath. None of those powerful city-states were better off or larger than Judah and Israel, yet enemies conquered all of them. If those mighty places could not save themselves, the leaders of Israel had no reason to think they were safe.

The leaders pushed the thought of God's day of judgment far out of their minds. Because they convinced themselves that punishment was distant, they felt free to set up unjust courts and oppress the poor. In doing so, their wicked choices were actually bringing the day of disaster closer.

The prophet highlights the lazy, over-the-top luxury of the wealthy ruling class. They stretched out on costly couches inlaid with ivory and dined on the very best lambs and stall-fattened calves. While their neighbors were suffering, these leaders cared only about indulging their own appetites.

The wealthy leaders played tunes on stringed instruments and made up songs for their drinking parties. They compared themselves to King David, claiming to be skilled creators of music. But while David used instruments to praise God, these men only used music to entertain their selfish desires.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this passage condemns using musical instruments in church worship, arguing that believers should only sing without instruments.

notes.meaning: The leaders drank their wine from huge bowls usually reserved for sacred offerings instead of regular cups. They pampered their bodies with the most expensive oils for their celebrations. Yet through all their merrymaking, they felt no grief over the moral ruin and coming collapse of the nation of Israel, here called Joseph.

God declares that their punishment will match their selfish lifestyle. Because these nobles made themselves first in rank and first in luxury, they will be the very first prisoners marched into exile. Their loud parties and lazy lounging on couches will suddenly come to an end.

The Lord God makes a solemn promise sworn on His own life and character, meaning it cannot be revoked. He utterly despises the arrogant pride of Israel, including the luxurious palaces built through greed and oppression. Because of their rebellion, the Lord will hand over the capital city of Samaria and everything in it to their enemies.

Even if ten men manage to survive a military attack and shelter together in one home, all of them will still die from disease or starvation. In normal times, at least a few people in a large group might survive an outbreak. Here, God's judgment is so complete that not a single person is spared.

A surviving relative arrives to carry out and burn the dead bodies because the usual undertakers have died. When he calls into the dark corners of the house to see if anyone is left, the final survivor whispers that no one remains. The relative quickly commands silence, terrified that speaking the name of the Lord might bring down more judgment.

The Lord Himself gives the command for total destruction to fall on the land. Great mansions belonging to the rich will be smashed to pieces, and small houses of the poor will be cracked into rubble. When God's judgment strikes, no building or social standing will protect anyone.

Amos uses two common-sense questions to expose the leaders' foolishness: horses cannot run on steep rocks, and farmers do not plow rocky cliffs with oxen. Yet the rulers were doing something just as unnatural and harmful by corrupting public justice. They turned fair judgment into poison and transformed honest living into bitter suffering for the poor.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate the second question as 'Does one plow the sea with oxen?' by slightly adjusting the Hebrew word spacing to describe an impossible task.

notes.meaning: The people were bragging about winning border battles and capturing the towns of Lo-debar and Karnaim in their own strength. Amos uses wordplay to expose their pride, since Lo-debar sounds like the phrase for 'nothing' and Karnaim means 'horns,' an ancient symbol of strength. They were boasting that their own might had won victories that were completely meaningless before God.

The Lord warns that He is preparing the Assyrian empire to march against Israel as His tool of judgment. This invading army will crush the land from Lebo-hamath in the far north all the way to the southern desert stream near the Dead Sea. The entire nation, from one border to the other, will experience the devastation of war.
